sections.text: ### What Survives

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: Senet is the oldest known board game with surviving physical evidence: game boards and pieces found in Pre-dynastic Egyptian tombs (~3100 BCE). Faience (glazed ceramic) game pieces. Elaborate game boxes found in 18th dynasty tombs — Tutankhamun's tomb contained four senet boards.

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: The **critical problem**: we do not have a rule set from the formative period. All rule reconstructions are scholarly inference from board iconography, hieroglyphic references, and the game's religious context.

sections.text: ### Discovery

sections.text: Sir Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Cemetery of Ur (Iraq) 1922-1934, finding multiple game boards in the "death pits" — mass burial sites of queens with retinues. The game dates to ~2600-2400 BCE. The boards are inlaid with shell, lapis lazuli, and red limestone — prestige objects for wealthy owners.

      appears alive can die 30 moves later based on
      global board state. A "weak" looking position

sections.text: ### AlphaGo and AlphaZero Significance

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: AlphaZero (2017): trained only against itself with no human game data, learned chess in 4 hours and Go in 8 hours, defeated Stockfish 8 (chess) and AlphaGo (Go). The implications for human Go theory: centuries of established joseki (corner sequences) that humans treated as near-optimal were shown to be suboptimal. AlphaZero preferred different opening patterns entirely.

sections.text: ## Common Confusion Points

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: **"Senet rules are known"**: They are not. Multiple scholarly reconstructions exist (Kendall, Crist, Bell) with different interpretations. Rules likely varied by period and region. Tutankhamun's senet board ≠ Pre-dynastic senet.

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: **"Go is 4,000 years old"**: Traditional attribution; not archaeologically confirmed. Spring and Autumn period (~500 BCE) is the earliest reliable evidence. The 4,000-year figure is cultural mythology — important culturally but not historically verified.

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: **"The ball game sacrifice — losers were killed"**: Both winners and losers are depicted being sacrificed in different sources. The Maya Hero Twins (Popol Vuh) are ballplayers who are killed and reborn. Some courts show captive warriors (not ballplayers) being sacrificed. The simple "losers die" narrative is modern oversimplification.

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: **"Mancala is a children's game"**: Oware at tournament level requires deep calculation. Bao (4×8 board) has never been solved computationally. The sowing mechanic enables combinatorial depth that is not obvious from watching casual play.

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: **"Astragali are fair dice"**: Not at all. Bone shape creates systematic non-uniform probabilities. Ancient users did not identify this as a bias — they simply assigned values to common and rare throws.

metadata.title: Ancient Games - From Senet to the Mesoamerican Ball Court

sections.text: **"Go superseded chess in AI difficulty"**: Both were hard in different ways. Chess required breakthrough evaluation; Go required learned intuition. Go's branching factor (~250) vs chess (~35) made brute-force approaches fail faster. AlphaGo's contribution was not greater compute — it was the insight that learned value and policy networks could replace evaluation functions and search pruning.

Tang dynasty China:
  Paper money develops later in China; Tang-period play likely
  involved paper slips, money-like tokens, or denomination concepts
  rather than Song-dynasty jiaozi in the strict sense.
  Money amounts to physical tokens with:
    - Distinct values (ranks)
    - Combinational rules (which beats which)
    - Trading between players (gambling)

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

  Whether paper money folded INTO game cards, or whether

  Cards predate their first European appearances by 400+ years

sections.text: ## Section 4: Trick-Taking Games — The Core Mechanic

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: Trick-taking is the fundamental mechanic of an enormous family of games. Understanding it unlocks Bridge, Whist, Hearts, Spades, Euchre, Pinochle, Skat, and Canasta variants.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
```
TRICK-TAKING MECHANIC
══════════════════════

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
BASIC STRUCTURE:
  N players. One player leads a card.
  Others must "follow suit" (play same suit if possible).
  If you can't follow suit: play any card (including trump).
  Highest card of led suit wins the trick — UNLESS
  a trump was played, in which case highest trump wins.
  Winner of trick leads next.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
COMPLETE INFORMATION PARADOX:
  In Bridge/Whist, the trick-taking phase is perfect
  information IF cards have been played openly.
  But it's bidding that makes it IMPERFECT INFORMATION —
  you don't know partner's cards during the auction.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
INFORMATION FLOW:
  After all 13 tricks, both teams know what both
  hands contained. A good player DEDUCES partner's
  holding from bidding and play patterns.
  This is Bayesian inference: update distribution
  of unknown cards given observed plays.
  Formally: a factor graph where variables are unknown
  hands and factors encode bid + play constraints —
  each card played is a conditioning event, same
  structure as belief propagation on a graphical model.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
VARIANTS ON CORE:
  HEARTS: avoid tricks (negative scoring) for heart cards
          and Queen of Spades — the "shooting the moon"
          strategy (take ALL hearts + QoS = 26 points
          AGAINST opponents) is the game's elegant exception.
  SPADES: bid the exact number of tricks you'll take.
          Sandbag penalty for taking too many ("tricks"
          beyond bid accumulate as bags; 10 bags = penalty).
  EUCHRE: 24-card deck, bower system (J of trump suit =
          highest, J of same color = second highest).
```

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge
Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
KEY RULES:
  No bidding. Trump is random (last card).
  Partners sit opposite each other.
  Must follow suit if possible.
  Partnership communication: ONLY through card play.
    Playing the highest card in a suit signals
    "lead this suit to me." Playing low signals
    "I don't have strength here."

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
EDMOND HOYLE (1672-1769):
  "A Short Treatise on the Game of Whist" (1742) —
  FIRST systematic rulebook for any card game.
  Hoyle documented the probabilities, strategies,
  and conventions of Whist scientifically.
  "According to Hoyle" entered English as a phrase
  meaning "according to the established rules."
  Hoyle later wrote similar books for Backgammon,
  Piquet, Chess, and Quadrille.
```

sections.text: ### The Hoyle Significance

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
Hoyle's treatise represents a pivotal moment: the application of systematic, probabilistic thinking to a recreational game. Before Hoyle, card game "strategy" was informal. Hoyle codified:
- Which cards to lead (strong vs passive leads)
- How to signal to partner through card order
- Probability calculations for remaining cards
- When to take vs duck (allow opponent to win) tricks

sections.text: This is the direct ancestor of the massive body of card-game strategy literature that followed.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

BRIDGE EVOLUTION
═════════════════

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
WHIST (17th century):
  No bidding. Trump = last card.
  Pure play skill.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
BRIDGE WHIST (~1895-1904):
  Declarer names trump suit before play.
  Dummy hand visible. No bidding on contract size.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
AUCTION BRIDGE (1904):
  Players BID for the right to name trumps.
  Highest bidder names trumps AND commits to making
  that many tricks. Partnership bidding: can bid higher
  to "protect" partner's suit.
  Critical innovation: the auction phase as communication.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text:
CONTRACT BRIDGE (Harold Vanderbilt, 1925):
  Played during a steamship crossing (SS Finland,
  October-November 1925, Vanderbilt and friends).
  Key innovations:
  1. VULNERABILITY: a team with a partial score is
     "vulnerable" — higher penalties for failing contracts,
     higher bonuses for making slam.
  2. SCORING REFORM: Only tricks bid AND made count toward
     game (in Auction Bridge, extra tricks beyond bid
     counted toward game too).
  These two changes made the bidding phase *strategically
  critical* — you must bid what you can make, precisely.
```

sections.text: ## Common Confusion Points

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: **"Tarot cards are an ancient occult tradition"**: They are 15th-century Italian gaming cards. Antoine Court de Gébelin invented the "ancient Egyptian" mythology in 1781 — over 350 years after tarot was created as a game. The Rider-Waite "standard" divination deck was designed in 1910. Tarot is actively played as a trick-taking game in France and Italy today.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: **"Blackjack basic strategy guarantees you win"**: Basic strategy minimizes the house edge to ~0.5%, but you still lose in the long run. The only positive-EV approaches require card counting + bet spreading — and casinos ban counters.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: **"Card counting is cheating or illegal"**: Neither. You're using your brain to track public information. Nevada law (and most jurisdictions) allows casinos to refuse service to anyone — they can ban you, but you've committed no crime.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: **"The standard deck has 52 cards because of the year"**: Folk etymology. The 52-card deck descends from the Mamluk 52-card deck through Spanish/Italian/French transmission. The 52-week correlation is coincidental.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: **"Whist and Bridge are essentially the same"**: Structurally related but Bridge added the entire auction system, dummy hand as fully visible, vulnerability scoring, and game/slam bonuses. These transforms make Bridge several orders of magnitude more strategically complex than Whist.

metadata.title: Card Games - From Tang Dynasty Paper to Contract Bridge

sections.text: **"Gin Rummy and regular Rummy are the same"**: Gin Rummy is a specific 2-player variant of Rummy with 10 cards, a "knock" mechanism, and its own distinct scoring. "Rummy" refers to the broad family; Gin Rummy is the most widely played member in the US.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text: The earliest precursor to billiards was an outdoor lawn game in France (and possibly England), roughly contemporary with similar games. Players used curved mallets (from French *mail* or *maille*, related to the English word "mall" as in Pall Mall, London — named for the game played there). Balls were pushed through hoops or wickets.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text: The connection to both modern billiards and croquet is direct: the same game moved indoors to tables (becoming billiards) while also remaining outdoors in refined form (becoming croquet). Pall Mall in London was a famous venue for the outdoor game, giving its name to the street.

  Players started using the handle end of the mace
  (the thin end) for shots near the cushion.
  "Handle end" → cue (from French queue = tail)
  Eventually the cue replaced the mace entirely.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text: American pool (pocket billiards) developed separately from the English tradition. The American game emphasized pocketing object balls more than the English hybrid carom/hazard play.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
CONTINUOUS POOL / STRAIGHT POOL (14.1, ~1910):
  15 balls, rack 14 when 14 are pocketed (leave last ball).
  Call every shot (call pocket, call ball).
  Score 1 point per pocketed ball.
  Play to 125, 150, 200, etc.
  Considered the most demanding pool game.
  Still the standard for serious pool evaluation.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
NINE-BALL (~1920s):
  9 balls only. Must strike lowest numbered ball.
  Winner pots the 9-ball (by any legal means —
  combination shots, scratch-and-re-rack...).
  Fastest form. TV-friendly. Professional standard.
```

sections.text: In mathematical physics, "billiards" is a canonical model in dynamical systems theory. A point particle reflecting specularly off boundaries produces trajectories whose behavior depends entirely on boundary geometry:

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
ELLIPTICAL TABLE:  Integrable (no chaos)
  All trajectories either pass through both foci
  or never pass through either. Caustics are confocal
  ellipses/hyperbolas. Fully predictable.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
RECTANGULAR TABLE:  Integrable
  Trajectories reduce to torus flow via unfolding.
  Ball path = straight line on the torus.
  Rational angle → periodic orbit.
  Irrational angle → ergodic (fills table uniformly).

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
SINAI BILLIARD:  Chaotic
  Square table with circular obstacle in center.
  Sinai (1970) proved ergodicity — foundational
  result in ergodic theory.
```

sections.text: The practical billiards table (rectangular with pockets) is integrable in the mathematical sense, but cushion deformation, spin, and friction introduce nonlinear effects that make long-range prediction difficult — the "chaos" of real billiards is physical, not geometric.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text: The physics of billiard ball collisions is interesting enough to be taught in physics courses:

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
This principle is used for position play:
  To get cue ball to a specific spot after potting,
  aim the object ball and use 90-degree rule to predict
  cue ball path. Spin modifies this.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text:
PHYSICS OF SPIN DECAY:
  A spinning ball slows in spin as it rolls (rolling friction).
  The distance the ball travels before spin disappears
  determines how far from the contact point the cue ball
  ends up in its "natural" position.
  Professional players calculate these distances intuitively
  through thousands of practice hours.

sections.text: **"Pool and billiards are the same"**: Pool is pocket billiards (American tradition). Billiards in its strict sense is carom (no pockets). "Billiards" is also used colloquially to mean any cue sport, but technically they're distinct games.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text: **"Snooker is played in the same pockets as pool"**: Snooker pockets are smaller (about 3.5 inches vs 4.5-5 inches for pool). Snooker balls are also smaller (52.5mm vs 57.15mm for pool). The tighter pocket on a larger table makes snooker demanding in a different way from pool.

metadata.title: Billiards, Pool, and Snooker - From Ground to Green Baize

sections.text: **"The 147 break happens often in professional snooker"**: It's extremely rare. Over the entire professional era (~80+ years), there have been perhaps 200+ official 147s total — many by Ronnie O'Sullivan. A full season of professional snooker might see 5-10 maximums at most.

sections.text: ### The Landlord's Game (1903)

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: The origin of Monopoly is one of game history's most significant cases of intellectual property erasure:

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
```
MONOPOLY ORIGIN STORY
══════════════════════

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
ELIZABETH "LIZZIE" MAGIE (1866-1948):
  Inventor, stenographer, political activist.
  Patented "The Landlord's Game" in 1903.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
PURPOSE: Explicitly designed to demonstrate
  Henry George's "Single Tax" economic theory:
    - Land values increase due to societal improvements,
      not landowner effort.
    - Therefore, land value should be taxed, not labor.
    - Georgism: one tax on land, abolish other taxes.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
Magie's intent: show players that the monopolist rules
  create misery, while the landlord rules create prosperity.
  A teaching tool with TWO economic models embedded.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
BOARD LAYOUT (original):
  Circular track. Properties to purchase.
  "Mother Earth" square (later: Free Parking/Go).
  Luxury Tax. Jail. Railroad squares.
  Atlantic City street names were NOT in Magie's original —
  those came from Darrow's Atlantic City version.
```

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: ### The Charles Darrow Myth

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
```
WHAT PARKER BROTHERS TOLD THE PUBLIC:
  Charles Darrow (1889-1967), unemployed engineer from
  Philadelphia, "invented" Monopoly during the Depression.
  Sold it to Parker Brothers in 1935. Became first
  board game millionaire. A classic American success story.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED:
  1. Magie's game spread informally from ~1903 onward,
     passed hand-to-hand in progressive and academic circles.
  2. Charles Todd of Atlantic City had a version with
     Atlantic City street names by ~1929.
  3. Darrow LEARNED THE GAME from the Todds in ~1932.
  4. Darrow made a commercial version, patented it (1933-1935).
  5. Parker Brothers bought Darrow's version.
  6. Parker Brothers also purchased Magie's ORIGINAL PATENT
     for $500 with no royalties and no public credit.
  7. Parker Brothers then sued multiple people for infringing
     Darrow's patent, effectively suppressing the game's
     actual history.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
THE SUPPRESSION WAS SUCCESSFUL FOR DECADES:
  Magie's role was known to game historians but
  largely unknown to the public until Ralph Anspach
  (the "Anti-Monopoly" creator) fought a decade of patent
  litigation and uncovered the history through discovery.
  Mary Pilon's book "The Monopolists" (2015) brought
  the full story to mainstream awareness.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
LIZZIE MAGIE'S COMPENSATION:
  $500. No royalties. Monopoly has since sold to
  approximately 1 billion people across 300+ versions
  in 47 languages.
```

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: ### Monopoly as Game Design

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
```
MONOPOLY AS STUDY IN BAD DESIGN
══════════════════════════════════

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
Ironically, the game that's played by the most people
is also widely cited by game designers as a study
in what NOT to do:

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
ELIMINATION MECHANICS:
  Players who go bankrupt are eliminated from the game.
  The eliminated player must then watch others play
  for hours. Eliminated players have no agency or fun.
  Modern design principle: keep players engaged throughout.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
LUCK-DOMINANT IN DETERMINING WHO WINS:
  Dice rolls for movement. Dice rolls for chance/community chest.
  Property acquisition depends heavily on what you land on.
  Skill is minimal — bargaining is the only significant decision.
  Long game: with skilled negotiators, outcomes still largely
  determined by early dice luck (who lands on Boardwalk/Park Place
  vs. who doesn't).

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
RUNAWAY LEADER:
  The rich get richer mechanically. No comeback mechanism.
  Once a player has monopolies and houses, the game
  becomes a waiting game for the richer player to win.
  This is mechanically correct for the monopolist rules
  Magie designed — but it's a poor entertainment experience.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
HOUSE RULE PROLIFERATION:
  The published rules are NOT what most families play.
  Common house rules: Free Parking jackpot, $200 for landing
  ON Go (not passing it), auctions when someone declines
  to buy (the ACTUAL RULE most families don't know).
  The official auction rule makes the game significantly
  shorter and more strategic.
  The Free Parking jackpot house rule extends the game
  dramatically (money that should leave the system stays in it).
```

sections.text: ### Kriegsspiel (1824) — First Serious Wargame

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution
Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
INVENTOR: Lt. Georg von Reisswitz (and father Johann)
  Berlin, 1812 (early version) → 1824 (published version)

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
PURPOSE: Military training tool. Prussian Army adopted it.
  General von Müffling: "This is not a game! This is
  military training! I shall recommend it to the whole army."
  Used to train officers in tactical and strategic decisions
  without actual combat.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
MECHANICS:
  Scale map of battlefield.
  Blocks represent units (company/battalion level).
  Referee/umpire mediates the rules.
  Dice for combat outcomes.
  Movement rates based on troop type (infantry/cavalry/artillery).
  Fog of war: units only visible when in detection range.
  Two-player (or team-vs-team).

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
THE UMPIRE INNOVATION:
  Kriegsspiel introduced the "referee" or "umpire" role —
  a neutral party who knows the full state of the game but
  mediates between players who only know their side.
  This is the direct ancestor of:
  - Dungeon Master/Game Master in D&D
  - Narrator in narrative tabletop RPGs
  - Admin/moderator in online war sims

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
MILITARY ADOPTION:
  Prussia: mandatory for officer education ~1870s
  Germany: used to plan WWI (Schlieffen Plan analyzed via wargame)
  US military: adopted after observing German efficiency
  Modern: military war gaming still used (Naval War College)
```

HEX-AND-COUNTER WARGAMES
══════════════════════════

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
AVALON HILL (founded 1952, Baltimore):
  Charles Roberts publishes "Tactics" (1952) — first
  mass-market commercial wargame.
  "Gettysburg" (1958): first game about specific historical battle.
  Hex grid + cardboard counters = the standard format.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
WHY HEX GRIDS:
  Square grids create diagonal movement asymmetry
  (diagonal = 1.414× distance, creating unrealistic movement).
  Hexagonal grids: the unique regular tiling with isotropic
  adjacency — all 6 neighbors equidistant, eliminating the
  diagonal asymmetry inherent in square grids.
  Combat resolution: compare attack/defense factors + die roll.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
SPI (SIMULATIONS PUBLICATIONS INC, 1969-1982):
  James Dunnigan, SPI. Prolific publisher.
  Strategy & Tactics magazine (included game with each issue).
  ENERGY: computer modeling + game design combined.
  SPI published hundreds of titles before going bankrupt.
  Acquired by TSR (D&D publisher) then Avalon Hill.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:

  Compass Games, Victory Point Games, Cole Wargames.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
CHAINMAIL (1971): Gary Gygax + Jeff Perren.
  Medieval miniature combat rules for Avalon Hill era gamers.
  First rules for man-to-man combat scale (not battalion).
  Added fantasy supplement: spells, monsters, heroes.
  Direct predecessor to D&D.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
DAVE ARNESON (Minneapolis):
  Created "Braunstein" campaign with Chainmail rules.
  Key innovation: PERSISTENT CHARACTER.
  Rather than controlling an army, each player controlled
  a SINGLE CHARACTER who accumulated experience and survived
  between sessions. The dungeon as the scenario.
  Characters grew in capability over multiple sessions.
  This is the RPG innovation.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
THE REVOLUTIONARY STRUCTURE:
    - No board (the Dungeon Master describes the environment)
    - No fixed victory condition
    - Characters persist and grow across sessions
    - Collective narrative creation
    - Dungeon Master as referee, narrator, and world creator
    - Combat resolution via dice + modifiers

sections.text:

sections.text: ### The Mechanism Taxonomy

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: Modern board game designers think in terms of mechanisms — the structural building blocks that can be combined to create games. This taxonomy emerged from the BGG community and designer discourse:

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
```
GAME MECHANISM TAXONOMY
════════════════════════

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
WORKER PLACEMENT:
  Players have limited "worker" tokens.
  Each worker occupies one action space (blocking others).
  Actions: gather resources, build structures, convert goods.
  Examples: Agricola, Viticulture, Everdell, Terraforming Mars.
  Mechanism origin: largely invented by Uwe Rosenberg (Agricola).

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
DECK-BUILDING:
  Players start with weak identical decks.
  Purchase better cards from a shared market.
  Shuffle purchased cards into deck.
  Your deck improves each shuffle cycle.
  Examples: Dominion (2008, originator), Thunderstone, Ascension.
  Key innovation (Donald X. Vaccarino, Dominion):
    The deck IS the game state, not just the tool.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
AREA CONTROL:
  Players place units on a map.
  Control regions for points or resources.
  Combat determines contested regions.
  Examples: Risk (classic), Small World, Blood Rage, Twilight Imperium.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
COOPERATIVE GAMES:
  All players vs. the game system.
  Win or lose together.
  Communication about strategy is unrestricted (usually).
  Examples: Pandemic, Spirit Island, Arkham Horror, Gloomhaven.
  Innovation: "traitor" variant (one player is secretly working
    against the group) — Battlestar Galactica, Dead of Winter.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
LEGACY GAMES:
  Permanent changes to the game based on outcomes.
  Write on the board, tear up cards, add stickers.
  Game evolves over multiple sessions (a "campaign").
  Each session is simultaneously repeatable (you own it)
    and irreversible (you changed it).
  Examples: Pandemic Legacy, Gloomhaven, Betrayal Legacy.
  First true legacy game: Risk Legacy (Rob Daviau, 2011).

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
ROLL-AND-WRITE:
  Roll dice (or draw cards). Write results on personal sheet.
  Minimal interaction; simultaneous play.
  Examples: Yahtzee (early), Wingspan (dice-drafting variant),
  Railroad Ink, Ganz Schön Clever.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text:
ENGINE-BUILDING:
  Build a system of synergizing components.
  Components generate resources that buy more components.
  Goal: achieve most efficient engine, then score.
  Examples: Wingspan, Race for the Galaxy, Gizmos.
```

sections.text: ## Common Confusion Points

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: **"Monopoly is the most-played board game because it's well-designed"**: Monopoly's ubiquity is a product of aggressive marketing by Parker Brothers and the suppression of alternatives. Its actual design is widely criticized by modern game designers for elimination mechanics, runaway leader problems, and luck dominance.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: **"The Landlord's Game had the Atlantic City properties"**: No. Atlantic City street names were added by Charles Todd's version, which Darrow learned from Todd. Magie's original had generic street names.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: **"RPGs require a board"**: D&D and most tabletop RPGs use no board. Space is described verbally by the Game Master. The "dungeon map" on graph paper is a player convenience tool, not a game component.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: **"Warhammer is a board game"**: Warhammer (Games Workshop, 1983) is a miniature wargame — tabletop war gaming with painted miniatures. The game space is a physical table with terrain models. It's distinct from board games (fixed game board) and RPGs (narrative focus). Warhammer 40,000 (1987) is the most commercially successful miniature wargame in history.

metadata.title: Modern Board Games - From Monopoly to the Eurogame Revolution

sections.text: **"Legacy games are just expansions"**: Legacy games permanently change between sessions — stickers applied, cards destroyed, story elements revealed. An expansion adds content; a legacy game changes irreversibly. You can't undo a Pandemic Legacy decision. Risk Legacy lets you name locations and permanently alter the board. Each copy of a legacy game becomes unique after play.

sections.text: ### Spacewar! (1962) — MIT, PDP-1, Steve Russell

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: The first canonical video game was not made by a corporation. It was made by MIT graduate students with unauthorized night access to a $120,000 PDP-1 — the first commercial computer with a real-time CRT display.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games
08 - Video Games

sections.text:
**Cultural significance:**
Stewart Brand's famous 1972 Rolling Stone article "Spacewar: Fanatic Life and Symbolic Death Among the Computer Bums" coined the term "hacker" in its celebratory sense. The thesis: Spacewar! demonstrated that computers were not just tools for the military-industrial complex — they could be **toys**, and that reframing would eventually drive the entire consumer software industry.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: The MIT hacker ethic: information wants to be free, code should be shared, and the playful exploration of a system's limits is the highest form of intellectual engagement. This culture flows directly to the early Homebrew Computer Club → Apple → Linux → open source → GitHub lineage.

sections.text: ### Ralph Baer and the Magnavox Odyssey (1972)

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: While MIT hackers were using million-dollar mainframes, Ralph Baer at Sanders Associates (defense contractor) was asking a different question: can you display something interactive on a consumer TV?

sections.text: Baer filed his patent in 1966. This matters because Atari's Nolan Bushnell later claimed he conceived Pong independently — but he had demonstrably seen the Odyssey demo at a trade show before tasking Al Alcorn with building Pong. Magnavox won the subsequent patent infringement suit and collected royalties from nearly every console manufacturer for two decades.

sections.text: ### Atari Pong (1972 arcade / 1975 home) — From Analog to Chips

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: Nolan Bushnell's genius was not invention but commercialization. Pong's arcade cabinet (1972) used a custom IC to implement what Baer had done with discrete components. The home version (1975) went further: a single dedicated chip, the "Pong on a chip" (AY-3-8500 by General Instrument), did everything — generating video signals, tracking score, detecting collisions.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: This is the transition that matters: **discrete logic → dedicated silicon → programmable CPU**. Each step made games cheaper to produce and more complex to play.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: The F2P model is textbook price discrimination: whales/dolphins/minnows self-select into spending tiers, each paying close to their reservation price. This is first-degree price discrimination achieved without negotiation — the IAP menu acts as a screening mechanism. Combined with network effects (more players improve match quality, which drives engagement and spending), F2P is a two-sided platform problem where the free players are the product that retains the paying players.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **App Store Price Compression:** When the App Store launched in 2008, Myst — the benchmark prestige game — cost $5.99. Within six months, $.99 was the ceiling for perceived "fair" pricing. The entire industry collapsed to $0.99 or free + IAP. The discovery algorithm rewarded new releases, creating a treadmill where sustainable revenue required IAP rather than unit sales.

sections.text: **Genshin Impact (2020)** as the inflection point: a console-quality open-world RPG, free to play, monetized through gacha character pulls. Made $2.8B in first year. sections.text: ### Key Design Theorems

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **Sid Meier:** "A game is a series of interesting decisions." Corollary: any mechanic that doesn't present a genuine decision is padding.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **Richard Garfield on luck vs. skill (Magic: The Gathering):** A game of pure skill (chess) is solved once one player outskills the other enough. A game of pure luck (slot machine) has no depth. The optimum for sustained engagement: luck provides variance that keeps weaker players competitive, while skill provides consistent expected-value advantage over time. MTG draft format: the best players win ~70% over large sample sizes despite random card draws.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **Will Wright's possibility space:** SimCity's cities, The Sims' stories, Spore's creatures — Wright designs systems that generate possibility spaces for players to explore, then steps back. The "game" is the space itself, not a prescribed path through it. Contrast with linear narrative games where the designer controls the journey.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text:
**Roguelike design principles:**
- **Permadeath** — not punishment, but anti-save-scumming. Forces genuine decisions because reversibility is removed. A save-anywhere system means the player can always undo mistakes; permadeath means mistakes have weight.
- **Procedural generation** — Binding of Isaac, Hades, Spelunky all generate layouts differently each run. The skill is in reading and adapting to novel configurations, not memorizing optimal paths.
- **Meta-progression** — modern roguelikes (Hades model) add permanent unlocks across runs, providing the "progression loop" layer above the "core loop."

sections.text: ## Common Confusion Points

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **The Atari crash was about quality, not technology.** The common narrative is "home consoles killed arcades" or "the industry was disrupted." The actual cause was Atari's decision to license anything — ET, the Atari 2600 Pac-Man port — without quality review. The market became indistinguishable from the toy aisle because it literally shared shelf space with non-games. Nintendo's business insight was that the quality floor matters for platform trust, not just individual title quality.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **"3D" in the SNES/Mode 7 era was not 3D.** Mode 7 applies an affine transformation (scale + rotation, no perspective correction) to a single background plane. F-Zero's road is Mode 7. Super Mario Kart's track is Mode 7. The depth illusion comes from scaling a top-down texture, not from rendering a 3D environment. True perspective-correct 3D on SNES required DSP coprocessors in the cartridge (Super FX chip for Star Fox).

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **Blast processing was marketing.** The Motorola 68000's ability to continue address-bus operations during DMA was real. Sega's advertising department turned this into "BLAST PROCESSING" implying a dramatic performance advantage. The actual difference mattered only in specific bandwidth-constrained scenarios, not as a general multiplier.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **CD-ROM did not kill cartridges because of capacity alone.** The decisive factor was manufacturing cost economics: $1–2 to press a CD vs. $15–25 to manufacture a cartridge. This gave Sony a retail margin advantage of $13–23 per unit sold, which compound across a catalog of 100+ games represents hundreds of millions in developer/publisher relationship advantages. The capacity (700 MB vs. 32–64 MB) mattered for FMV and audio, but the real kill shot was margin economics.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **Esports salaries are not equivalent to traditional sports.** The top LoL/CS:GO players earn $500K–$2M annually, comparable to mid-tier professional athletes in minor sports. But team organizations are often unprofitable — the Overwatch League franchise fee was $20M for rights to a competition that many teams are now exiting. Prize pool visibility (TI at $40M) obscures that most esports players earn $30K–$80K, similar to minor league baseball. The economics are still stabilizing.

metadata.title: 08 - Video Games

sections.text: **Battle royale as genre did not originate with PUBG.** The BR mode in Minecraft (Hunger Games servers) predated PUBG by 5+ years. The DayZ battle royale mod (Brendan Greene/PlayerUnknown, 2013) directly preceded PUBG. Greene created the standalone PUBG after working on H1Z1: King of the Kill. The genre had multiple predecessors; PUBG operationalized it at commercial scale.
